title: The Shunammite's Land, Hazael's Tears, and Judah's Decline
summary: The Shunammite woman, back from seven years in Philistia during a famine, appeals to the king for her land just as Gehazi is telling him how Elisha raised her son, and her property is restored. In Damascus, Elisha tells Hazael that his sick master Ben-hadad will die and weeps as he foresees the evil Hazael will do to Israel as king; Hazael smothers Ben-hadad and takes the throne. Meanwhile in Judah, Jehoram and then Ahaziah, both tied by marriage to the house of Ahab, do evil, yet the LORD preserves a lamp for David.
story: This chapter closes the main cycle of Elisha stories and opens the political upheaval of chapters 9 through 11. It gathers loose threads. The Shunammite of chapter 4 returns, and the famine of 4:38 may well belong to the seven-year famine told of here. The commission God gave Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:15-17), to anoint Hazael king of Aram, Jehu king of Israel, and Elisha as prophet, now reaches its second stage: Hazael comes to power, and Jehu's turn follows in chapter 9. The second half of the chapter shows the cost of Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab. Jehoram of Judah married Ahab's daughter, and the house of Ahab's ways have now reached the throne of David.
historical:
Hazael seized the throne of Damascus around 842 BC. Assyrian records confirm his reign: an inscription of Shalmaneser III describes Hazael as the son of a nobody, the Assyrian way of naming a usurper with no royal father, and reports battles against him in 841 BC and later. Hazael became the most dangerous enemy Israel faced in the second half of the ninth century, taking territory east of the Jordan (10:32-33) and later threatening Jerusalem (12:17-18). Many scholars attribute the Aramaic Tel Dan Stele, found in northern Israel in 1993 and 1994, to Hazael; in it an Aramean king boasts of killing a king of Israel and a king of the house of David, probably Joram and Ahaziah, whose deaths 2 Kings 9 attributes to Jehu.

In Judah, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat reigned about 848 to 841 BC, after a period of co-regency with his father. Edom, which had been subject to Judah, broke away and set up its own king (verses 20-22), and Libnah, a town in the lowlands toward Philistia, also revolted. Second Chronicles 21 adds further detail about Jehoram's reign, including the murder of his brothers and raids by Philistines and Arabs. His son Ahaziah reigned about a year (841 BC). The two dates given for Ahaziah's accession, the twelfth year of Joram here (verse 25) and the eleventh in 9:29, likely reflect different ways of counting a king's first partial year.
cultural:
The Shunammite's seven years abroad left her land vulnerable to being taken by the crown or by neighbors, since property without its owner present could be treated as abandoned. Her appeal to the king follows the right of any subject to seek royal justice. The king's interest in Elisha's great deeds and the timing of her arrival are presented as God's providence: she comes in at the very moment Gehazi is telling her story. That Gehazi, struck with skin disease in chapter 5, is speaking with the king here suggests either that the episodes are not in chronological order or that he was allowed such contact; the text does not say.

Consulting a foreign prophet about a king's illness was not unusual, and forty camel loads of gifts was a display of royal generosity meant to secure a favorable oracle. Hazael's phrase for himself, a mere dog, was a conventional expression of humility in the ancient Near East, found also in other ancient letters, including the Lachish letters from Judah's last years. The violence Elisha foresees in verse 12 (burning fortresses, killing young men, dashing infants, and ripping open pregnant women) describes the terrible customs of ancient warfare that the prophet Amos later condemned in Aram's and Ammon's treatment of Gilead (Amos 1:3, 13).
literary: The chapter has three parts. The first (verses 1-6) is a short story of providential timing that brings the Shunammite's tale to a satisfying close. The second (verses 7-15) is one of the most emotionally charged scenes in the Elisha cycle. The prophet's long stare, until Hazael is ashamed, and his sudden tears, are unusual details for this spare narrator. Elisha's answer in verse 10 is also puzzling: the Hebrew text as written can be read as tell him, you will not recover, while the traditional reading followed by most translations says tell him, you will surely recover, with the addition that he will in fact die. The third part (verses 16-29) returns to the regnal formulas of the book of Kings, reporting two reigns in Judah in the standard pattern and setting the scene at Jezreel, where both kings, Ahaziah and Joram, will meet their end in the next chapter.

outline.t: Elisha weeps before Hazael, who kills Ben-hadad and reigns
Jehoram's reign over Judah and Edom's revolt
Ahaziah of Judah joins Joram of Israel against Hazael

doctrines.note: The Shunammite arrives exactly as her story is being told, and the king restores her property with all its produce. God's care for her did not end with the raising of her son; it continued through famine, exile, and a bureaucratic loss.

Judah's king does evil, “Yet for the sake of His servant David, the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah” (verse 19). God's promise to David holds even when David's descendants fail, because it rests on his faithfulness.

God knows the evil Hazael will do and still names him king over Aram. The LORD rules over the rise of nations, even enemy nations, without approving their cruelty; Elisha's tears show that foreknowing judgment is not the same as delighting in it.

words.note: Nir, lamp. The LORD had promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants (verse 19; compare 1 Kings 11:36 and 15:4). A burning lamp in a house signified that the family still lived there and had a future. The image keeps David's line alive through the darkest reigns of the book.

Bakah, to weep. The prophet's weeping is unexpected. He is not weeping for Ben-hadad but for Israel, because he sees what Hazael will do to it. The verb is used of mourning for the dead and of intense grief, and here it shows a prophet who carries the pain of the judgment he announces.

Gur, to live as a sojourner or resident foreigner. The Shunammite sojourns in Philistia for seven years (verses 1-2), as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob's family had sojourned in foreign lands during famine. A ger, a sojourner, had limited rights, and her return to reclaim her land is a small picture of restoration after exile.

christ: Elisha weeping over the suffering Israel will endure has a striking counterpart in Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem as he approached it, foreseeing that its enemies would surround it and dash it to the ground with its children (Luke 19:41-44). Both prophets grieve the judgment they announce, and both show that God's word of judgment is not spoken coldly. The promise of a lamp for David, which keeps Judah from destruction in verse 19, runs toward the New Testament's announcement that God has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69) and the angel's promise that Mary's son would receive the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32). The link is the promise itself, kept alive through kings who did not deserve it until the son of David who would reign forever.

hard.q: Did Elisha tell Hazael to lie to the king, or encourage him to murder?
hard.a: Elisha tells Hazael to say that Ben-hadad will recover, while revealing that he will die. There are two main ways to understand this. One reading holds that both statements are true in different senses: the illness itself would not have been fatal, but Ben-hadad would die by another cause, and Elisha discloses both. Another reading follows the written Hebrew text, which can be read as tell him, you will not recover, making Elisha's message plainly truthful; the traditional marginal reading, which most translations follow, gives the sense found in the BSB. As for murder, the text does not say that Elisha told Hazael to kill his master. Elisha foresees that Hazael will be king and weeps over what he will do; Hazael then chooses his own means. God's naming of Hazael as king (1 Kings 19:15) is no more an endorsement of his methods than God's use of Assyria later endorses Assyria's cruelty (compare Isaiah 10:5-12). The chapter holds together God's sovereign foreknowledge and human guilt for evil acts, without explaining fully how they fit.

questions: The Shunammite came to the king at exactly the moment her story was being told. Where have you seen God's timing in events you could not have arranged?
Elisha wept over the evil Hazael would do. How does a prophet's grief change how you hear God's words of judgment?
Judah was spared “for the sake of His servant David.” What does it mean for you that God's faithfulness can rest on someone else's covenant rather than on your own record?
